analysis.one_liner: Makes community college free and covers tuition at public four-year colleges for families earning under $125,000.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2017 and referred to the Senate's education committee, the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal-state program to eliminate tuition and required fees at every community college, and at public four-year colleges for students from families earning $125,000 or less. It also would have capped federal student loan interest rates (undergraduates at 5 percent), let existing borrowers refinance to current rates, and redirected any profits from the federal direct loan program into Pell Grants. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Every community college student (tuition and fees eliminated, no income test); students from working- and middle-class families earning up to $125,000 at public four-year colleges; all federal student loan borrowers, who could refinance old loans to current lower rates and would see new undergraduate loans capped at 5 percent; Pell Grant recipients, funded by federal loan program revenue; low-income and first-generation students, through expanded TRIO, GEAR UP, and Work Study; and tribal colleges, historically Black colleges, and other minority-serving institutions, which would get grants to cut tuition for low-income students.

how_it_helps.text: Eliminates tuition and required fees for all students at community colleges and two-year tribal colleges, with no income limit.
Eliminates tuition and required fees at public four-year colleges for students whose family income is $125,000 or less, with the threshold rising with average wages over time.
Cuts new federal undergraduate loan rates (capped at 5 percent) and lets current borrowers refinance outstanding federal loans to current rates at any time.
Requires the Education Department to send any revenue the federal direct loan program earns beyond its costs into the Pell Grant program.
Expands TRIO, GEAR UP, and Federal Work Study funding and reallocates Work Study money to campuses based on student need rather than historical formulas.

Provides grants to private historically Black colleges and minority-serving institutions that cut tuition for low-income students, and requires states that take the money to maintain instruction spending, need-based aid, and tenured faculty levels.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through roughly $41 billion authorized for the tuition program in fiscal 2018 plus $1.34 billion for minority-serving institutions and expansions of TRIO, GEAR UP, and Work Study; state governments, which must cover 33 percent of the tuition-elimination cost and maintain education spending as a condition of receiving federal funds; and the federal treasury, which gives up loan program profits that would otherwise offset costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers and participating state governments

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes about $41 billion per year for tuition elimination on top of roughly $5.4 billion in other higher education programs, a large new federal commitment whose long-term cost grows with enrollment and wages.
States must supply a 33 percent match and maintain prior spending levels, so the benefit reaches students only in states willing and able to pay; students in states that decline would get nothing.

The $125,000 income threshold extends free tuition well above the median family income, which critics would call a subsidy to families who can pay, and the same $125,000 threshold applies everywhere regardless of local living costs.
Participating colleges must reach 75 percent tenured or tenure-track instruction within five years and face restrictions on how funds are used, which some institutions would find difficult to meet.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is large and concrete: free community college for everyone and tuition-free public four-year college for most families, plus lower and refinancable loan rates. The costs are also real: tens of billions in federal spending each year, a mandatory state match that makes participation uneven, and a benefit threshold that includes families earning well above the median. The bill's design addresses the usual free-college objection (aid leaking to affluent families) less fully than a strict income cap would, but its maintenance-of-effort and faculty-quality conditions are more demanding than most similar proposals. Because it never received a hearing, none of these trade-offs was ever publicly tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2017 and sent to the Senate's education committee, it sat there with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Sanders introduced the College for All Act of 2017 on April 3, 2017, joined by Democratic Senators Harris, Warren, Blumenthal, Murphy, and Gillibrand.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The action record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the 115th Congress: no hearing, no committee markup, no vote, and no discharge petition.
The bill's cosponsor list totaled seven senators, all Democrats alongside the independent sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No new group gained a benefit; the status quo held, so students and families continued paying tuition and loan interest as before. Taxpayers were spared the program's cost, and nothing about how colleges are funded or how loans are priced changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo — students kept paying tuition and interest

against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee the bill was referred to, scheduled no hearing and no markup, leaving the bill to die without any committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or the independent sponsor, and the Republican-led committee never acted, but because no vote ever occurred the record shows no actual division of the two parties on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have replaced tuition revenue at community colleges and public four-year institutions with federal and state grants, while requiring maintained instruction spending and 75 percent tenured faculty. Students gain free tuition and institutions gain a stable public funding channel.

Free public community colleges would pull enrollment away from institutions that charge tuition for similar credentials, and the bill explicitly bars newly converted for-profit colleges from its minority-serving grants for at least 25 years.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit colleges (other than minority-serving institutions)
industries.note: A no-tuition public option would give students a free alternative, pressuring private colleges that depend on tuition revenue; private historically Black and minority-serving institutions were carved out and funded instead.
Federal undergraduate loan rates capped at 5 percent and the right to refinance old federal loans to current rates would make federal borrowing much cheaper, leaving private loans less competitive.
